visible.summary: Tuvalu demands real caution. Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced); no LGR; very small, tight-knit, church-centred society; no specifically documented anti-trans violence (population ~11,000). Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
visible.tangentialFactors: Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Tuvalu: documents the legal status — male same-sex conduct criminalised under colonial-era provisions.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tuvalu: traditional customs perpetuate religious and social discrimination including against women; no government abuses; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the Penal Code but no prosecutions.

Tuvalu Ministry of Health Global AIDS Progress Report 2017 (UNAIDS): the national HIV response, drawing on the Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study on HIV and STI risk vulnerability among key populations (including MSM and transgender Tuvaluans).

US Mission Geneva (22 Mar 2011): Tuvalu appears among roughly 80 signatory states of the UN joint statement recalling General Assembly resolutions on human rights, sexual orientation and gender identity; also lists Asia-Pacific Forum and Council of Europe mechanisms used to press the issue. Documents Tuvalu's 2011 diplomatic position; dated but on-topic.

GlobalGayz Tuvalu archive: aggregates news and reports incl. an OHCHR Human Rights Day op-ed urging states to decriminalise consensual same-sex relations, plus historical items on Tuvalu's colonial-era sodomy-law status. Useful as a dated context and pointer source rather than primary authority.

visible.summary: Solomon Islands is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years); no LGR; documented social hostility; weak state capacity post-Tensions; no open community infrastructure.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Solomon Islands: documents the legal status — same-sex conduct criminalised under colonial-era law, up to 14 years.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: no security-force abuses; violence and discrimination against women prevalent; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the penal code but no prosecutions.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: documents lengthy pretrial detention, corruption, violence against women - general context; no LGBT-specific abuses reported.
US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: documents the RAMSI assistance mission, the Lusibaea case, and general human-rights conditions - baseline assessment.

SIBC (8 Jun 2018): Governor General Sir Frank Kabui used his Queen's Birthday address to warn that 'same sex marriage cannot populate the world' — a dated official statement of elite hostility to recognition; no same-sex marriage law exists and Parliament has not legislated one.

Human Dignity Trust profile: Solomon Islands criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, maximum penalty 14 years' imprisonment (Penal Code provisions); the profile documents the colonial-law basis and the absence of recorded prosecutions in recent years.

Wikipedia reference summary: male and female same-sex sexual activity is illegal and punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, but the law is not enforced; LGBTQ people face legal challenges not experienced by other residents, with no relationship recognition or non-discrimination shield.

visible.summary: Nauru demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2016; tiny population (~12,000); no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; the asylum-detention legacy shaped its international image but not its LGBT law. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: US Mission Geneva (Mar 2011): publishes the full text of the Joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation & gender identity, delivered by Colombia on behalf of 84 countries — Nauru is among the signatories (with Fiji, Marshall Islands, Micronesia and others). For this record: dated evidence of Nauru's diplomatic position supporting SOGI rights.

Human Truth Foundation 'LGBT Rights Across the World' (Vexen Crabtree, 2025): the Vexen LGBT Equality Index ranks Nauru 101st at -0.10, far below top-ranked Germany/Spain at 4.88 and below most Pacific neighbours. For this record: a comparative-index placement for Nauru.

The Guardian (29 May 2016), headline-level (article body did not survive retrieval — nav shell only): 'Nauru decriminalises homosexuality and suicide' — the 1899 Queensland-derived criminal code provisions repealed, replacing them including attempted-suicide provisions. For this record: the dated decriminalisation event.

Kaleidoscope Trust Nauru country page: Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016 but same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal; intersex and transgender people have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and no employment-discrimination protection for LBTI people; Nauru supported the 2011 UN HRC Joint Statement, and its last CEDAW state report (2016) contained no LBTI-specific information. For this record: the current legal-status snapshot for trans/intersex people specifically.

visible.summary: Palau demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2014; small, US-associated, tourism-dependent; no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2014 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: US Mission Geneva (22 Mar 2011): Palau is among the 84 countries on whose behalf Colombia delivered the joint Human Rights Council statement calling for an end to violence and human-rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity — early dated diplomatic signal of Palau's position.

Erasing 76crimes (16 Oct 2014): Palau decriminalised homosexuality — per Human Dignity Trust, Palau's Attorney General confirmed the new Penal Code (signed by the President in April 2014) dropped the sodomy offence formerly at s.2803 Ch.28 'Sex Crimes' Title 17 (up to 10 years' imprisonment); at its 2011 UPR Palau had accepted recommendations to repeal criminalisation and combat LGBT discrimination; the move dropped the global anti-sodomy country count to 79.

Scoop/OHCHR Pacific piece (c. 2011): lists Palau among 70+ Pacific/global jurisdictions with laws criminalising same-sex relations still on the books, and records that Palau and Nauru accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts during their Human Rights Council UPR appearances — documenting Palau's stated commitment to repeal.

visible.summary: Benin is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but 76crimes documents that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace; the Hirondelles Club provides safe housing for LGBT youth fleeing family violence. No LGR, no anti-discrimination law; community organises underground.
visible.tangentialFactors: Anti-gay lynching pattern — trans people are among the most visible targets of perceived-LGBT violence; same-sex conduct itself is legal.
visible.localsOnly: No LGR and no anti-discrimination law — resident-facing gaps; the Hirondelles Club safe housing serves local youth.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Lynching pattern is documented climate, not statute.

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (9 Apr 2024): the Hirondelles Club at Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth in Benin since about 2020 — a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed; the report's framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin. For this record: current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised anywhere in Benin, but SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. For this record: the current statutory baseline — legal but entirely unshielded, no recognition pathway.

US State Department 2023 Country Report (Benin): the law does not explicitly prohibit SOGIESC discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. For this record: official US assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

Washington Blade (31 Aug 2015), commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups: LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. For this record: regional religious-institution hostility including Benin — dated 2015, treat as context not current-state evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (8 May 2012): interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo (political sociology/medical anthropology, EHESS Paris) citing evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits' record of women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom (modern Benin); frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import. For this record: historical baseline supporting the localsOnly framing that today's statutory legality sits on pre-colonial practice, not recent liberalisation.

visible.summary: Togo is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “immodest or unnatural acts” (3 years); limited recent enforcement evidence but documented discrimination and violence; no LGR.
visible.tangentialFactors: “Immodest or unnatural acts” criminalised (3 years) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust country profile (fetched this session): Togo criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment plus a fine — the core exposure fact for a visitor.

AAEC Togo + Synergia alternative report to the UN Human Rights Committee (June 2021): the Togolese association works on HIV within MSM-TG populations under the National Strategic Plan 2016-2020, documents LGBT rights violations across Togo and francophone West Africa, and provides legal/judicial support to victims — evidence of an active civil-society documentation and assistance channel.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Togo: the law prohibits 'acts against nature committed with an individual of one's sex' (widely understood as same-sex conduct) and also the 'promotion of same-sex conduct', reaching advocacy and gender identity expression; the law was enforced, and violence/threats targeting LGBTTQI persons were listed among significant human-rights issues — official current-law + enforcement read.

Washington Blade (Aug 31, 2015): interviews with LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria (conducted 14-31 March 2015) include a Togo section — the author returned to Lomé, visited the site of a 2008 attack on him, and reports the capital's police are 'particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists', a rare on-the-ground note naming TOURIST exposure.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Togo: documents security-force torture, impunity, and 'official and societal discrimination... against members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for Togo: significant issues include cruel treatment, harsh prisons, arbitrary detention, criminal libel enforcement, and 'crimes involving violence or threats of violence targeting lesbian, gay, bisexual...' persons.
